newsitem.title: USA: Phelps Dodge sees good growth, stable prices in '97.
newsitem.headline: Phelps Dodge sees good growth, stable prices in '97.

text.p: Copper demand is set to remain relatively strong this year with prices maintaining current levels, but a surplus of metal will hit the market in the second half of the year, Phelps Dodge Corp's chairman, president and CEO Douglas Yearley said.

"We are hopeful that we will have reasonable stability in the price around where we are now," Yearley told Reuters. "I think the fundamentals support pricing in the 90 cents to $1.10 (per pound zone)."
Cash costs at Phelps are "under 60 cents a pound", and every 10 cent move in copper's price causes a $1.60 per share earnings change in a full year.
"We expect, on a very provisional basis, the U.S. demand for copper this year will continue to be quite strong."
Phelps forecasts copper demand to grow three to 3.5 percent this year, "with a bias towards the 3.5 percent", Yearley said, up from about three percent last year.
Phelps will produce 1.6 billion pounds of copper this year, up from 1.55 billion in 1996, rising a further 110 to 120 million pounds in 1998 as Candelaria is expanded.
Phelps is the world's biggest maker of copper rod, and produced a record 1.35 billion pounds last year, making the company a relatively minor cathode seller in net terms.
Most of Phelps' output is sold in the United States.
"We have just changed our goal to producing 2.2 billion pounds of copper by the year 2002," Yearley said. Phelps has some six to seven percent of the world's copper market.
Yearley expected the market to end 1997 in a "modest surplus" of 150,000 to 200,000 tonnes, though he cautioned that demand was constantly being underestimated, while supply was often overestimated.
"But I don't think we have overestimated demand at 3.5 percent," Yearley said, adding that supply this year was set to rise 5.5 to six percent.
